items.bodyEn: Between Kanaya and Nissaka the road climbs Sayo-no-Nakayama, ranked with Hakone and Suzuka among the Tōkaidō's three hardest passes. Hiroshige's Nissaka print shows travelers staring at a boulder set in the middle of the steep road: the 'night-crying stone', which local legend says once called out in a mother's voice. Travelers bought sweets beside it.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō 'Nissaka: Sayo no Nakayama'; Tōkaidō meisho zue (1797)

items.bodyEn: In 1186 the monk-poet Saigyō, nearly seventy, crossed this pass a second time on his way east and wrote: did I ever think, grown old, to cross it again? Life itself has brought me here, Sayo-no-Nakayama. The poem entered the Shin Kokinshū and made the pass a place every literate traveler wanted to see.
items.ja: {年|とし}たけてまた{越|こ}ゆべしと{思|おも}ひきや{命|いのち}なりけり{小夜|さよ}の{中山|なかやま}
items.kana: としたけてまたこゆべしとおもひきやいのちなりけりさよのなかやま
items.sourceNote: Shin Kokin wakashū, book 10 (travel poems), Saigyō

items.bodyEn: わけ, written 訳, is the noun form of 分ける 'to divide, sort apart'. Sort a tangle into its parts and you see how it hangs together, so わけ came to mean the reasoning behind a thing. The kanji 訳 was borrowed later; its own meaning is 'translate'. Every 〜わけだ at this station still carries that sense of falling into place.
items.sourceNote: Daijirin / Daijisen, entry わけ【訳】 (from 分ける)

items.bodyEn: The わけ family denies at three strengths. 〜わけがない flatly rules something out: 彼が来るわけがない, no chance. 〜わけではない softens a partial denial: 嫌いなわけではない, it's not that I dislike it. 〜わけにはいかない says circumstances forbid it even if you could: 今日は休むわけにはいかない. Pick by how much door you want to leave open.
items.kana: きらいなわけではない。
